Doctors mental health

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When you have to be a hero to everyone, how do you cope when you take off your cape? We look at Doctors mental health

Summary:
A medical doctors job requires that they are perfect, if they make a mistake it could mean someone dies. Mental illness is seen as an unacceptable weakness, one a medical professional can not afford. With a crumbling public health system and fears around the new NHS system, doctors on performing under more pressure than ever before and in some cases with less resources. Medical doctors across the country are in distress, but what is being done about it?

1. Stacey Rassouw is a neurosurgeon at Frere hospital. Medicine is in her family, her dad was a nurse. In 2013 after years of battling silently he took his own life.
2. Couple A are both medical doctors, he suffered a mental breakdown in the beginning of the year. It was the compounded effect of personal issues and professional stress that landed him in the in patient unit.
His wife talks openly about her husbands mental health and how they have tried to hide it.
3. Case study B from Cassey

After her fathers suicide and years of watching colleagues suffer in silence Stacey decided to team up with SAMA to create a campaign that is starting with a hashtag #mefirst to make doctors aware that they are not alone. State facilities should have EAP programs to support doctors mental health, but most hospitals do not have these programs in place. The frere doesn’t. Stacey has lost many colleagues over the years and has a good understanding of the complexity of he issue around doctors mental health

Cassey from SADAG will shed light on all the reasons why doctors legally and personally feel the pressure to not disclose any mental health issues.
SADAG will provide stats and solutions, how do they get help?
We will film the doctors at home, without their white gown, without their armour. And then also film them working.

Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:00 Dr Stacy I’m on my way it’s an acute stroke
Hello
Hello Angel
Do your lift mama
2 00:10 Macfarlane Doctors are real life superhero’s, we rely on them when we are sick to take away the pain and save our loved one. What happens when they need saving?
3 00:18 Voice With the crumbling state health system, the pressure on doctors has become unbearable. They are working extremely long shifts, running on no food and trying to give patients the best care that they can with extremely limited resources.
4 00:38 Dr. Hayley Shh...
Sorry my angle, okay.
Shh
5 00:44 Dr Hayley interview You are dealing with life and death and when it gets to that point when you have done your resuscitation and you fail, I’ve had days when I would be in ICU one minute trying to resuscitate a child and getting a phone call that says you need to come in and see these patients right now. I find that so challenging.
6 01:00 I think the hardest thing here is dealing with loss and difficulty, but you have to desensitise yourself in order to do your job and it’s not really who I am as a person to do that.
7 01:09 Voice Dr. Hayley Harker has been a medical officer and paediatric surgery for 7 years. She gave everything she had to being the doctors she has always been wanting to be but this year the price became too high
8 01:22 Interview with Hayley and Macfarlane Macfarlane: Hayley when does it all become too much for you?

Dr. Hayley: We had a colleague who actually had a breakdown and left for a while and so we started to explore this issue of mental health a bit more and we actually had someone to come in and speak to us about burnout. I remember sitting in her lecture and realizing that I tick all the boxes, everything she said it was everything I felt
9 01:44 Voice over A burn out is not something that happens overnight, it creeps up on you months or years of intense pressure. You get insomnia, a lack of appetite, irrational anger and a general apathy for life. As it gets worse it develops into anxiety and depression. For Hayley, what really made her realize she was in trouble was when she started out isolating herself from her family
10 02:09 Interview with Dr Hayley Hayley: I was just really irritated with everything all the time and lacked patience with my family and to me that wasn’t okay and I wasn’t willing to do that with them. I actually remember taking a walk with my husband and saying I can’t do this to you anymore.
11 02:29 Voice over Dr. Chuma Makunga has worked in ER units and some of the most over capacitated hospitals in Gauteng. Recently her work with state rape clinics had a serious impact on her emotional well-being.
12 02:42 Dr. Chuma interview You are only human, you become affected because when you are in the rape centre you have to listen to the story unfolding. You have to listen to how the rape came about and you go home watching your back, you go home not knowing when you are going to be the next rape victim and you just have to pick your pieces and heal yourself and you sometimes go to work leaving your family at home and you are scared what’s going to happen to your children at home.
13 03:17 Voice over After over 10 years of staying strong and not letting the work get to her, Dr. Chuma had to take a leave of absence this year in order to save her mental health.
14 03:28 Dr Chuma I have had a period of a depressive episode. You know you start being angry internally and you start feeling you think you are angry at the work process. But when it reaches the peak you are angry at the system, you are angry at yourself, you are angry at the patient, you are angry at anyone who is trying to talk to you.
15 03:50 Voice over Dr. Stacy Rossouw is the only state neurologist in the buffalo city municipality. She’s on call 24 hours a day.
16 03:58 Dr Stacy Rossouw I think the one thing that’s a challenge for all of us, is often you are judge, the jury and the execution when you have to make those decisions of who are the ones that are going to get lifesaving treatment in a resource environment
16 04:15 Voice over Stacy was born into a family of medical professionals so the pressure to succeed started at a young age.
17 04:22 Dr. Stacy You always feel that if you are not perfect then you are failing. There’s no middle ground. We are passionate about what we are doing and we should be warry that that very passion and calling doesn’t affect you. I have been experiencing first hand my dad committed suicide in 2013. He was a nurse and he worked in the emergency department a very stressful environment. In that very same token and same time that he... my brother had to aparant suicide attempts.
18 04:51 Dr Stacy in the ward But you must scan her. Are we going… when last did you see and she was fine last week?
19 04:59 Voice over While south Africa doesn’t have any studies specify to suicide rates for doctors. A study in the US has shown that doctors are two times more likely to commit suicide than any other population group
20 05:11 Dr. Chuma Doctors are facing a whole lot of mental health issues quietly. We have been trained to be hero’s and we therefore behave like hero’s we go through our own pain, both physically and emotionally quietly because we are expected to be able to save everyone else and we are only seen not to be coping when we commit suicide sadly.
21 05:38 MacFarlane link With 40% of South African doctors suffer burnouts which untreated leads to depression and suicide we ask why are these hero’s suffering in silence?
22 05:49 Dr Stacy I’ve been seen as the hero so how can the hero say that he or she has a crack in their armour?
23 05:57 Dr Hayley I definitely get the feel even in training you are expected to be super human because if you are feeling a certain way you are not coping with something then it’s like this wasn’t for you and you don’t fit the profile.
24 06:09 Voce over SADAG has taken a vested interest in the well-being of medical professionals after receiving an over whelming response to their help line they set up for medical student in 2017. Cassy chambers is the operational director for SADAG
25 06:22 Cassey Chambers SADAG I think culture has been created where they are not encouraged to speak about it, I don’t deal with emotional issues, I’m fine, I will carry on and its seen as a weakness and here you got these super humans by everyone around them has built them up that they can’t crack and they can’t fall apart and that there is no place for it at the determent of the doctor
26 06:44 Macfarlane and Dr. Chuma Macfarlane: when you going through all of this why didn’t you reach out and try and get help sooner?

Dr. Chuma: Initially I thought I was coping, I’m quit a strong person and I have survived quit a lot of adversities so I would not have reached out for help sooner because I didn’t think I needed help. I only realised I needed help when I snapped.
27 07:06 Macfarlane After losing her father to suicide and almost her brother, neurologists Stacy Rossouw decided enough is enough.
28 07:13 Voice over Together with the eastern cape branch of the South African Medical Association she launched the MEFIRST campaign to open dialogue amongst medical professionals and helped them see that it is safe to speak out, that they are not alone.
29 07:27 Dr. Stacy We just took it upon ourselves and we said no more, we don’t want to hear about doctors committing suicide it’s an initiative to bring about dialogue and starting the engine with the doctors and with both government and non-governmental organisations
30 07:44 Cassey and Macfarlane Macfarlane: How can doctors get help?

Cassey: Really encouraging them to talk out and if they don’t feel comfortable amongst their colleagues there are support structures and specialists who are willing to help them and they can also phone anonymously and speak to a councillor at SADAG
31 07:57 Voice over After her proceeding treatment Dr. Chuma Makunga has tried to put her family first by spending more time at home taking care of them.

32 08:06 Dr. Chuma It affects your family, terribly. The people who suffer the most are the people who are the doctor’s family and and I wonder if we are about to truly be the best of the parents that we designed by God to be.
33 08:23 Voice over Since she was a little girl Hayley knew all she wanted to be was a doctor. She wanted to save lives but now she’s battling with a heavy decision of whether or not to leave the profession forever and what would that look like for her?

34 08:38 Dr. Hayley You know at the moment if I look at it and what it looks for now the image is so blurred compared to what I pictured it to be in the current sort of situation I’m like I’m ready to walk away

Macfarlane you’re done?

Dr. Hayley: But I think if I would stand in the future retrospectively I think I that would hurt, to know that’s all I wanted and then it wasn’t what I expected.
35 09:04 Voice over But for now, she has returned to work and has put measures in place to make sure that she’s taking care of herself so that she can take care of her patience.
36 09:12 Macfarlane and Hayley interview Macfarlane: What are you doing to cope?
Dr. Hayley: I have stopped doing overtime, I’ve started eating my lunch when I feel hungry, going to the bathroom when needing to go the bathroom, stepping outside when you feel you need to breathe those simple human basic things and its crazy how we feel guilty about that because we feel like because people have been here waiting since 6 in the morning we are not allowed to be human
37 09:33 Macfarlane and Dr. Chuma Macfarlane: if doctors continue to being silent what will eventually happen?

Dr. Chuma: what is happening will continue happening. We will snap one by one, we will commit suicide one by one, we will resign on the spot and walk away from the system one by one or we will continue cringing our teeth and carrying the burden and wanting to be seen as hero’s until we drop dead one by one as we do
